questions.stem: A person has been fasting for 48 hours. Their body has used up most of its glycogen stores. Which respiratory substrate will the body increasingly rely on for energy?

options.text: Amino acids from new protein synthesis
Lipids (fats) broken down from adipose tissue
Water stored in body tissues
Vitamins and minerals from the liver

questions.explanation: When glycogen stores are depleted, the body turns to lipids (fats) stored in adipose tissue as the next major respiratory substrate. Fats contain more energy per gram than carbohydrates and provide a long-term energy reserve.

questions.stem: A scientist measures the respiratory quotient (RQ) of a person and finds it is approximately 0.7. Which substrate is the person most likely using for respiration?

options.text: Carbohydrates, which have an RQ of 1.0
Proteins, which have an RQ of about 0.9
Lipids, which have an RQ of approximately 0.7
A mixture of all substrates equally

questions.explanation: The respiratory quotient (RQ) is the ratio of CO₂ produced to O₂ consumed. Lipids have an RQ of approximately 0.7 because they contain relatively more hydrogen and less oxygen than carbohydrates, requiring more O₂ for complete oxidation.

questions.stem: Glucose is considered the body's preferred respiratory substrate. Why is glucose used first before fats or proteins?

options.text: Glucose releases more energy per gram than any other substrate
Glucose is easily transported in the blood and quickly broken down to release energy
Fats and proteins cannot enter the mitochondria
Glucose is the only substrate that can be used in anaerobic respiration

questions.explanation: Glucose is the preferred substrate because it is soluble, easily transported in the blood, and can be rapidly broken down. Although fats release more energy per gram, glucose is more readily available and can be used in both aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

questions.stem: An athlete on a high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet exercises at moderate intensity. Compared to an athlete on a normal diet, how would their CO₂ output differ for the same energy release?

options.text: They would produce more CO₂ because fats contain more carbon
They would produce less CO₂ relative to oxygen consumed, as fats have a lower RQ
CO₂ output would be identical regardless of substrate
They would produce no CO₂ because fats do not contain carbon

questions.explanation: Fat oxidation has a lower respiratory quotient (RQ ~0.7) compared to carbohydrate oxidation (RQ = 1.0). This means less CO₂ is produced per molecule of O₂ consumed when respiring fats, even though both processes produce CO₂.

questions.stem: In severe starvation, the body begins to break down proteins from muscle tissue for use in respiration. Why is this a last resort for the body?

options.text: Proteins contain no usable energy
Breaking down structural and functional proteins damages tissues and impairs body functions
Protein respiration produces toxic carbon dioxide
Proteins can only be used in anaerobic respiration

questions.explanation: Proteins have essential roles as enzymes, structural components, and in immunity. Breaking them down for energy means losing these vital functions, leading to muscle wasting, weakened immunity, and organ damage. The body preserves proteins as long as other substrates are available.
